title: The AI Layoff Trap
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Computer and Information Science and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: The AI Layoff Trap
detail.abstract: If AI displaces human workers faster than the economy can reabsorb them, it risks eroding the very consumer demand firms depend on. We show that knowing this is not enough for firms to stop it. In a competitive task-based model, demand externalities trap rational firms in an automation arms race, displacing workers well beyond what is collectively optimal. The resulting loss harms both workers and firm owners. More competition and "better" AI amplify the excess; wage adjustments and free entry cannot eliminate it. Neither can capital income taxes, worker equity participation, universal basic income, upskilling, or Coasian bargaining. Only a Pigouvian automation tax can. The results suggest that policy should address not only the aftermath of AI labor displacement but also the competitive incentives that drive it.

title: Data Empowerment: A Study on the Impact of Big Data Analysis Capability on Organizational Resilience
affiliations: Guiyang University, Guizhou Minzu University and Guizhou Minzu University

detail.title: Data Empowerment: A Study on the Impact of Big Data Analysis Capability on Organizational Resilience
detail.abstract: Enhancing resilience in group is a key measure for manufacturing enterprises to cope with operational risks and achieve high-quality development. In the digital age, empowering enterprise development with data has received widespread attention, but existing research has paid little attention to the relationship between big data analysis capabilities and organizational resilience. Based on the dynamic capability theory and resource-based view, a theoretical model of the impact of big data analysis capability on organizational resilience was constructed using first-hand survey data from 346 middle and senior managers in manufacturing enterprises, based on the "capability resource environment" framework. Research has found that the ability to analyze big data has a significant positive impact on organizational resilience; Redundant resources, technological uncertainty, and market uncertainty all play a positive moderating role in the relationship between big data analysis capabilities and organizational resilience; Further analysis of the economic consequences reveals that big data analytics capabilities can improve corporate economic performance by enhancing organizational resilience. The research conclusion has important theoretical and practical significance for deepening the study of the antecedents and situational mechanisms of organizational resilience, and enhancing the organizational resilience of manufacturing enterprises in China.

title: Fostering Technology Acceptance in sports virtual training system through Gamification-Driven Interaction Optimization
affiliations: Jinling Institute of Technology and City University of Macau

detail.title: Fostering Technology Acceptance in sports virtual training system through Gamification-Driven Interaction Optimization
detail.abstract: Digital technology is widely applied in sports for environmental simulation, motion detection, data analysis, and diagnostic feedback, yet Sports Virtual Training Systems (SVTS) often suffer from low user technology acceptance due to cumbersome interaction workflows and high operational complexity. Drawing upon gamification theory and the emotional design framework, this study proposes a gamification-driven interaction optimization approach across visceral, behavioral, and reflective levels. A comparative experiment was conducted with 360 participants stratified into professional, semi-professional, and amateur athletic proficiency groups. Questionnaires assessed perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and behavioral intention. Results indicate that the experimental group scored significantly higher than the control group across all three dimensions, confirming the approach's efficacy in enhancing technology acceptance. Subgroup analysis revealed heterogeneous effects: amateur users exhibited significant improvements in all dimensions, semi-professional athletes demonstrated significant gains in perceived usefulness and behavioral intention, while professional athletes showed no significant change. These findings underscore the effectiveness of the proposed optimization pathway and emphasize that athletic proficiency moderates its impact, with greater benefits observed among lower-skill users. The approach offers actionable design implications for SVTS interaction optimization and suggests that design strategies should be tailored to the target population's overall skill level.

title: The Mandatory Labeling Regime for Generative AI as a Placebo : Performative Regulation Destined to Fail
affiliations: University of Macau, Nanchang University, Renmin University of China and

detail.title: The Mandatory Labeling Regime for Generative AI as a Placebo : Performative Regulation Destined to Fail

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by Meiji University (Grant No. 4122242013), and University of Macau (Grant No. YC372192).

detail.abstract: This paper critically examines the mandatory labeling regime for generative AI, arguing that it functions as a "regulatory placebo" destined to fail. Triggered by global technological panic, jurisdictions worldwide have hastily enacted labeling obligations to precisely demarcate human creations from AI-generated outputs. However, this reactive "emergency administration" lacks both a solid jurisprudential foundation and practical effectiveness. The study highlights that generative AI's high fluidity, immateriality, and increasing decentralization—especially via open-source local models—enable widespread technological evasion. This traps regulators in a dilemma of "structural selective enforcement," as tracking all violations becomes systemically impossible. Furthermore, from a jurisprudential perspective, penalizing unlabeled but otherwise harmless AI-generated content lacks a legitimate basis of punishability. Without infringing on substantial legal interests, such regulation alienates into a formalistic compliance shackle. Additionally, forcing AI to maintain artificial "non-human traces" contradicts the technology’s inherent evolutionary goal of anthropomorphic language capabilities, thereby sacrificing model robustness. Ultimately, the paper warns against this regulatory fever, emphasizing that symbolic labeling mandates fail to mitigate actual risks and may conversely erode the fundamental authority of the rule of law.

title: Compliance Checking for Decentralized Applications
affiliations: University of Camerino, University of Camerino, University of Camerino, University of Camerino, University of Camerino and University of Camerino

detail.title: Compliance Checking for Decentralized Applications
detail.abstract: While decentralized applications adoption has surged in several domains, the smart contracts implementing them can diverge from their specified logic. To address this issue, the data generated during the execution of smart contracts can provide valuable insights into the actual behavior of an application, enabling its analysis. For this reason, we employ compliance checking to audit decentralized applications based on their execution data. To enable such a technique, we provide a threefold contribution. Firstly, we present a domain-specific language, called CoBlock, to define compliance rules by relying on blockchain characterizations as a first-class citizen. Then we designed a visual rule modeling solution, CoBlockly, which abstract the underlying language, to facilitate auditors on building blockchain-specific compliance rules. Finally, we implemented a tailored framework for blockchain compliance checking to streamline the process of defining and checking compliance rules over decentralized applications execution data. The evaluation, which employs the real-world CryptoKitties decentralized application, includes accuracy and performance analysis in addition to a usability assessment to measure the feasibility and to demonstrate the practicality of the framework.

title: Dynamic Event-Triggered Control for Network-Based Offshore Platforms Under Cyber Attacks
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and National Cheng Kung University

detail.title: Dynamic Event-Triggered Control for Network-Based Offshore Platforms Under Cyber Attacks
detail.abstract: This article investigates the dynamic event-triggered control problem for networked offshore steel jacket platforms subject to stochastic cyber-attacks and time-varying actuator faults. To describe the hostile communication environment, a comprehensive stochastic attack model, incorporating both denial-of-service (DoS) and scaling attacks, is constructed using Bernoulli distributed random variables. To optimize limited communication resources in offshore remote monitoring, a novel dynamic event-triggered scheme is proposed to determine whether sensor data should be transmitted to the controller. Compared to traditional static triggering mechanisms, the proposed approach significantly reduces data transmission frequency while maintaining system performance. By constructing a Lyapunov-like functional with additional dynamic variables, sufficient conditions are derived in the form of linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) to guarantee the global exponential stability of the closed-loop system with a mixed 𝐻∞ and passivity performance index. Finally, a numerical simulation based on offshore platform parameters is provided to demonstrate the effectiveness and resilience of the proposed control strategy.

title: BEYOND FUNCTIONALITY: HOW EASE OF USE AND ENJOYMENT SHAPE CONSUMER DECISIONS IN E-COMMERCE
affiliations: Universitas Bina Nusantara, Bina Nusantara University (BINUS) - Binus Business School and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: BEYOND FUNCTIONALITY: HOW EASE OF USE AND ENJOYMENT SHAPE CONSUMER DECISIONS IN E-COMMERCE

keywords: Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology

detail.abstract: The emergence and growth of e-commerce make the business environment and competitiveness among companies fierce. Thus, this study wants to examine the key factors that influence consumers’ purchase intentions in Indonesia's rapidly expanding e-commerce sector. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) as foundational literature, this research integrates trust and perceived enjoyment to examine how perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and trust influence online buying behavior. Data for this study were collected through a purposive sampling method, gathering information from 204 valid respondents who actively shop online, which fits with our objective. The relationships between perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, trust, perceived enjoyment, and purchase intention were then analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results reveal that perceived ease of use and perceived enjoyment have a significant influence on purchase intention, while perceived usefulness and trust have no direct effect. However, perceived ease of use can mediate the relationship between trust and buying intention, suggesting that trust fosters a sense of convenience rather than immediate behavioral intention. These findings contribute to the refinement of TAM and UTAUT in saturated digital markets and offer practical guidance for e-commerce platforms to enhance usability and engagement.

title: Public Procurement in the Philippines: A Thematic Review of Governance, Compliance, and Performance
affiliations: and Lyceum Northwestern University

detail.title: Public Procurement in the Philippines: A Thematic Review of Governance, Compliance, and Performance
detail.abstract: Public procurement plays a pivotal role in governance and public financial management, as it determines how state resources are translated into essential goods, services, and infrastructure (OECD, 2019; World Bank, 2020). In the Philippines, Republic Act No. 9184, the Government Procurement Reform Act of 2003, standardized rules and procedures to promote transparency, accountability, and competitiveness. Despite these reforms, procurement continues to face challenges, including weak compliance, limited institutional capacity, and inefficiencies that erode public trust (COA, 2023; GPPB, 2023). The gap between policy intent and practice remains significant, with reforms often emphasizing compliance rather than performance and service delivery. This study adopts a desk-based, literature-driven approach (Bowen, 2009; Snyder, 2019) to provide a governance-focused synthesis of procurement in the Philippines. Drawing on secondary data-including COA reports, GPPB issuances, agency submissions, and international assessments such as the World Bank's MAPS-the review examines legal and institutional foundations, oversight mechanisms, compliance trends, and the performance of the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS). The analysis covers 24 line agencies between 2021 and 2023, highlighting systemic issues such as delayed reporting, fragmented digital systems, and capacity gaps, while also noting achievements in transparency, inclusivity, and fiscal accountability. A distinctive contribution of this review is its focus on the transition between RA 9184 and the new Government Procurement Reform Act (RA 12009), providing insights into institutional bottlenecks and behavioral responses during a period of legal change. Situating the Philippine experience within global and ASEAN procurement governance, the study identifies both benefits-such as enhanced transparency and broader supplier participation-and persistent constraints, particularly in digital integration and institutional coordination. Ultimately, the study underscores the need to move procurement reform beyond compliance toward strategic governance, integrating digital transformation, professionalization, and citizen-centered accountability to optimize procurement as a driver of efficiency, equity, and public trust.

title: Time as a strategic resource in the e-commerce boom: How consumption motivations shape consumer patience and self
affiliations: Guizhou Normal University, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen University and Shenzhen University

detail.title: Time as a strategic resource in the e-commerce boom: How consumption motivations shape consumer patience and self
detail.abstract: Online shopping, as a central feature of contemporary life, continually challenges consumers’ patience and self-control through its convenience and immediacy. Prior research on consumer patience has yielded inconsistent findings, largely due to fragmented and methodologically heterogeneous paradigms. To address these limitations, we develop a novel paradigm for studying consumer patience and integrate multimodal methodologies—including eye-tracking and web-scraped transactional data from major online retail platforms—to explore how different consumption motivations influence attentional allocation and self-construal, thereby shaping patience. Our results demonstrate that hedonic consumption motives enhance consumer patience: individuals engaged in hedonic pursuits allocate less attention to immediate-choice options and exhibit stronger relational self-construal. Our study overcomes the limitations of prior paradigms by introducing a novel framework that enables more rigorous and reliable analysis of multimodal consumer data and deeper insight into the psychological processes underlying consumer decision-making. The findings offer practical value for firms seeking to design more engaging marketing strategies, enhance consumer experience, and increase spending.

title: A Machine-Learning Framework for Real-Time Financial Anomaly Detection and Cash-Flow Forecasting in Enterprise Resource Planning Systems: Design, Implementation, and Empirical Evaluation
affiliations: National University of Sciences and Technology

detail.title: A Machine-Learning Framework for Real-Time Financial Anomaly Detection and Cash-Flow Forecasting in Enterprise Resource Planning Systems: Design, Implementation, and Empirical Evaluation
detail.abstract: Enterprise organisations increasingly generate voluminous transactional data within ERP ecosystems, yet traditional rule-based financial controls struggle to detect complex, temporally distributed anomalies and provide actionable forward-looking cash-flow intelligence. This article presents a comprehensive machine-learning (ML) framework integrated directly into an Oracle APEX ERP dashboard, designed to address both challenges simultaneously. The system deploys three complementary ML models—LightGBM for 30-day rolling cash-flow prediction, Random Forest for department-level expense forecasting, and XGBoost for transaction-level anomaly classification—operating over a corpus of 5,000 synthetic enterprise transactions spanning seven business units and ten vendor classes. On a 5,000-transaction synthetic corpus evaluated via an 80/20 temporal hold-out, all three models demonstrate strong proof-of-concept performance: the XGBoost anomaly classifier achieves AUC-ROC of 0.9523 (precision 0.923 at the HIGH-risk tier) on a rule-derived synthetic corpus and must not be interpreted as a generalised fraud detection benchmark; the LightGBM cash-flow regressor attains R2 = 0.9102 with a mean prediction stability index of 0.852 across a 30-day horizon; and the Random Forest expense forecaster achieves R2 = 0.8876 with MAPE of 7.4%. Net positive cash flow is correctly identified in 70% of forecast periods. Following a design science methodology (Hevner et al., 2004), these figures represent preliminary proof-of-concept benchmarks; external validity against real enterprise transaction data remains the subject of future work. Implications for enterprise FinTech architecture, model governance, and future reinforcement-learning extensions are discussed.

title: Beyond accuracy-centric ranking: A collaborative knowledge graph–guided deep learning recommendation framework balancing accuracy and diversity
affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, Dongbei University of Finance and Economics and University of Iowa

detail.title: Beyond accuracy-centric ranking: A collaborative knowledge graph–guided deep learning recommendation framework balancing accuracy and diversity
detail.abstract: Personalized recommendation has become an indispensable installation through which e-commerce platforms improve matching efficiency and enhance user experience. However, recommendation models that focus primarily on ranking accuracy may also narrow product exposure and generate repetitive recommendation lists. Although knowledge-graph-enhanced recommendation provides a useful way to enrich semantic information and alleviate sparsity, existing methods still face challenges in balancing recommendation relevance and diversity, especially under sparse and long-tail conditions. We propose KMAGNN, a collaborative knowledge graph-based recommendation framework that integrates relation-aware multi-head attention, gated residual propagation, and diversity-aware neighborhood regulation. The proposed framework captures heterogeneous semantic relations among users, items, and entities while stabilizing high-order message passing and reducing redundant semantic aggregation. In addition, dynamic negative sampling and a joint optimization scheme are introduced to support a more balanced recommendation objective. Experiments on multiple public datasets show that KMAGNN achieves a more favorable accuracy–diversity trade-off than competing methods and remains robust under sparse interaction settings. This study extends knowledge-graph-based recommendation by demonstrating how structured semantic modeling can support recommendation outcomes that are both relevant and diverse.

title: Trust, Risk, and Technology Acceptance in Online Retail: A Behavioral Perspective
affiliations: Peking University

detail.title: Trust, Risk, and Technology Acceptance in Online Retail: A Behavioral Perspective
detail.abstract: The acceleration of digital commerce has altered consumer buying behavior, but the uncertainty surrounding online transactions continues to influence user adoption. The paper explores the relationships among trust, perceived risk, and technology acceptance in online retailing, focusing on behavioral outcomes. Based on the synthesized concept of Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and perceived risk theory, the study will focus on the impact of cognitive and emotional inclinations of consumers on their readiness to use e-commerce platforms.,The study uses a structured survey dataset of online shoppers, which is then subjected to a high level of econometric testing with structural equation modeling (SEM) to determine the correlation among the key constructs, including perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, trust, financial risk, privacy concerns, and behavioral intention. The results indicate that trust is an essential mediator, increasing technology acceptance while simultaneously reducing the negative impact of perceived risk. Conversely, perceived risk, especially in regard to data security and uncertainty regarding payment, has a negative impact on both trust and adoption intentions. In addition, behavioral factors such as prior online experience, digital literacy, and platform reputation are found to mediate these associations.,The findings add to the existing body of research on digital consumer behavior by offering empirical insights into how trust and risk perceptions influence online retail adoption. In practice, the research emphasizes the need to enhance the security, transparency, and user-friendliness of e-commerce websites to establish consumer trust and encourage long-lasting engagement. These lessons are useful to policymakers, platform designers, and online retailers seeking to make digital markets more functional and inclusive in an economy increasingly driven by technology.

title: How Advanced Information Technologies Help and Hurt Crisis Response Adaptation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Delft University of Technology and Delft University of Technology

detail.title: How Advanced Information Technologies Help and Hurt Crisis Response Adaptation
detail.abstract: Climate change and geopolitical tensions demand increased adaptability from crisis-response supply chains. Advanced information technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain, have been proposed as tools for increased adaptability. However, recent evidence shows that such technologies can also lead to new vulnerabilities and risks, a phenomenon we refer to as \textit{maladaptation}. This paper analyzes the effects of information technologies on resource allocation in crisis-response supply chains and identifies the conditions under which maladaptation emerges. We develop an agent-based discrete-event simulation in which managers adapt their resource allocations and coordination structures in response to climate shocks and geopolitical emergencies, using different information technologies. Using exploratory modeling and rule induction, we conduct computational experiments to examine a sequential and convergent supply chain configuration. Both configurations use different information technologies and are exposed to disruption patterns. Rule induction reveals combinations of these technologies and characteristics of the disruption patterns under which efforts to reduce information delays and accelerate recovery may inadvertently decrease performance. The findings reveal two maladaptation profiles: broad and conditional maladaptation. Broad maladaptation refers to a technology that consistently underperforms the baseline regardless of disruption durations, whereas conditional maladaptation refers to underperformance restricted to specific disruption duration windows. The disruption pattern and supply chain configuration jointly moderate which profile a technology exhibits. Identifying these profiles advances understanding of maladaptation in crisis response supply chains as a condition-specific phenomenon.

title: Burnout to Balance Sheet: Quantifying the Financial Impact of Employee Mental Health on Productivity and Attrition
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Burnout to Balance Sheet: Quantifying the Financial Impact of Employee Mental Health on Productivity and Attrition

contentType.other: This submission is an original research paper and is currently unpublished. It is not under formal journal publication at this stage and is being submitted as an independent academic manuscript.

detail.abstract: Sustained performance pressure in contemporary work environments has elevated employee mental health to a strategic organizational concern. This study investigates how workplace burnout intersects with individual productivity and voluntary attrition, and seeks to assign concrete financial values to these relationships. Drawing on survey data gathered from 75 early-career professionals employed across India's finance, consulting, and startup sectors, the research identifies meaningful statistical associations between elevated stress, declining work output, and growing exit intent. Employees logging more than 50 hours weekly reported burnout levels substantially above the sample median, alongside a self-assessed reduction in productive output ranging from 15 to 25 percent. A financial model, grounded in survey-derived parameters and industry benchmarks, estimates that a 100person organization experiencing moderate burnout prevalence incurs an annual cost burden of approximately ₹57,60,000 from combined productivity erosion and replacement expenses. The study argues that mental health investment constitutes not merely a welfare measure, but a financially justified business strategy. Evidence-based recommendations are offered for organizations seeking to treat burnout as a manageable, quantifiable operational risk.

title: Market Resonance and The Inversion of Positive Obligations: Lessons from Tripathi

detail.title: Market Resonance and The Inversion of Positive Obligations: Lessons from Tripathi
detail.abstract: On March 13, 2026, the Supreme Court of India in Shailendra Mani Tripathi v. Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development declined to mandate paid menstrual leave, warning that such legislation could "backfire" by discouraging employers from hiring women. This article argues that the ruling generates two violations of binding international law. First, by citing predicted employer discrimination as a reason for inaction, the judgment inverts the positive-obligation architecture of CEDAW and core ILO instruments, under which anticipated discrimination is a trigger for regulation, not a defence of abstention. Second, by cautioning that recognition of menstruation may signal women's lesser capability, the reasoning reproduces the very stereotype that CEDAW Article 5(a) obliges states to dismantle. Situating these violations within Law and Political Economy and feminist political economy, the article introduces market resonance theory: a judicial mechanism through which market-first expectations are laundered into equality-law outcomes while maintaining the appearance of treaty fidelity. The analysis also identifies an internal contradiction with the Court's recognition of menstrual health as a fundamental right in Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Union of India six weeks earlier. The article concludes with a compliance framework that translates treaty duties into statutory design, cost-neutralisation, anti-retaliation architecture, and Article 5(a) stigma-reduction measures, aimed at resisting the interpretive drift through which market resonance operates.

title: When Carbon Pricing Backfires: Market Composition Effects
affiliations: Ryerson University, Western University and York University

detail.title: When Carbon Pricing Backfires: Market Composition Effects
detail.abstract: Carbon pricing aims to reduce emissions by contracting demand and inducing cleaner production. This paper shows that carbon pricing can backfire in markets with differentiated products and heterogeneous abatement technologies. When firms differ in baseline emissions and abatement responsiveness, a carbon price generates asymmetric pass-through that can raise the relative prices of cleaner products. Consumers then substitute toward products with slower price increases that remain more emissionintensive after abatement. A decomposition into scale, technique, and composition effects reveals that this market reallocation can dominate standard emissions-reducing channels. The analysis isolates a within-market mechanism that can reverse aggregate emissions reductions even under uniform carbon pricing.

title: Do EU funds reduce water pollution? Evidence from Spain
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Universidad Complutense de Madrid

detail.title: Do EU funds reduce water pollution? Evidence from Spain
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of EU funding on meeting the milestones of the European Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive using a staggered difference-in-difference design robust to heterogeneous and dynamic treatment effects. Specifically, we assess the extent to which the construction and improvement of urban wastewater treatment plants affect water quality in Spain, considering a set of parameters that measure the degree of water pollution. The results reveal that European regulations on water pollution have a statistically significant effect on the outcomes, reducing the probability of non-compliance with the Directive, as indicated by parameters related to oxygen demand and suspended solids.

title: The Impact of House Prices on Internal Migration: The Case of Spain
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), , International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: The Impact of House Prices on Internal Migration: The Case of Spain
detail.abstract: This paper studies how house prices shape internal migration across Spain’s provinces and the implications for the spatial allocation of labor. Using a gravity-style framework, we estimate the causal impact of destination and origin house prices on bilateral migration flows between 2007-2023. To address the potential endogeneity of house prices, we instrument provincial house prices with a Bartik-style predictor of external inflows of foreign migrants, allowing this housing demand shock to have larger price effects in provinces with tighter land constraints. The instrumental variable (IV) estimates show that housing costs constitute a significant barrier to internal migrants—a 10 percent increase in destination house prices reduces inflows by about 4.0 percent, while a 10 percent increase in origin house prices increases outflows by about 2.8 percent. These push effects of origin house prices are larger for foreign-born and foreign-born young individuals compared to natives. Rental costs have even stronger effects than home sale prices. A simple back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that if house prices in high productivity provinces had not grown faster than the inflation over 2017-23, about 63,000 more working-age individuals would have migrated to these provinces, as opposed to just 1,700 (in net terms) in practice. While the direct implied GDP gain would have been small—about 0.05 percent over this period, such gains would accumulate over time if regional divergence in house prices were left unaddressed. Furthermore, this estimate does not factor in the much larger gains from attracting a large number of recent foreign immigrants—not studied here—to the most-productive regions.

title: Controlling Collective Attention Flooding versus Focusing by Politicians
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Controlling Collective Attention Flooding versus Focusing by Politicians
detail.abstract: This paper asks when politicians spread communication across many issues (“flooding the zone”) rather than concentrate on few (“focusing”), and how this choice affects accountability. I develop a model in which a politician allocates a fixed communication budget across issues, while limited-attention watchdogs each examine one issue, and investigations occur only when enough watchdogs coordinate on the same target. In the baseline, breadth is chosen before issue qualities are realised and the disclosed issue set is fixed, isolating dilution from cherry-picking. Flooding is irrelevant when one watchdog can trigger scrutiny, but it reduces exposure when collective action requires collisions. The bad type’s incentive to flood increases with exposure penalties when investigation risk declines with breadth; under sparse collisions, the leading-order comparison is transparent. The model also provides sufficient conditions under which the good type focuses because depth is more informative. With endogenous curation, broad pooling can persist for small sophistication shares among partially sophisticated watchdogs. Journal of Economic Literature Classification Numbers: D72, D82, D83, C72.

title: Committee Size and Incentives in Political Selection
affiliations: University of Bath

detail.title: Committee Size and Incentives in Political Selection
detail.abstract: This paper studies committee-based selection when a winner is chosen by majority vote among committee members who make independent, noisy assessments of competing candidates. Each candidate chooses a costly investment that raises the probability of support from any given committee member. The main insight is a pivotality effect: marginal returns to investment arise only in states where the committee is evenly split, so that one member's decision can change the final outcome. As committee size increases, such pivotal states become less likely, which reduces the incentive to invest. At the same time, larger committees aggregate information more effectively, increasing the probability that the candidate with the highest investment is selected. These two forces generate a non-monotonic relationship between committee size and aggregate investment, and result in an interior committee size that maximizes candidates' investment.

title: External Demand Shock, Internal Geography and Intra-city Inequality the impact of tariff reduction-induced external demand shocks on China’s inequality
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics, Shandong University of Finance and Economics and Shandong University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: External Demand Shock, Internal Geography and Intra-city Inequality the impact of tariff reduction-induced external demand shocks on China’s inequality
detail.abstract: Utilizing a long-term artificial nighttime light dataset, we examine the impact of external demand shocks—stemming from tariff reductions faced by Chinese exporters—on China's intra-city inequality. Using a shift-share IV strategy, we find that a 1% increase in external shocks leads to a 0.014-unit rise in regional inequality. Furthermore, the dynamic effect of external demand shocks has begun to decrease since 2012. Geographic factors including external and internal geography have a significant moderating effect, and both population and capital agglomeration mediate the impact of external shocks on regional inequality. These findings underscore the need to direct targeted support to vulnerable groups and geographically disadvantaged regions.

title: Life Expectancy Beliefs and Their Economic Consequences in Kazakhstan
affiliations: World Bank, World Bank, Europe and Central Asia and World Bank

detail.title: Life Expectancy Beliefs and Their Economic Consequences in Kazakhstan
detail.abstract: Misperceptions about longevity may influence personal life-cycle choices, leading to significant macro-level effects. Yet, evidence of such economic consequences is scarce for developing countries. Using data from the 2025 round of the Listening to Kazakhstan survey, we find that respondents underestimate average life expectancy by 5–7 years. This bias varies by age, gender, smoking behavior, alcohol consumption, and subjective health status. We develop a theoretical model demonstrating that underestimating longevity reduces human capital investment, leads to earlier retirement, and depresses savings. When calibrated to Kazakhstan’s demographic and economic parameters, the model suggests that a 5-year underestimation of life expectancy generates welfare losses equivalent to as much as 1.6 percent of GDP, primarily through early labor market exit, reduced human capital investment, and inadequate retirement savings. Low-cost information campaigns to improve longevity awareness could therefore yield substantial economic benefits.

title: Third-party loss aversion reduces spectator redistribution
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Third-party loss aversion reduces spectator redistribution
detail.abstract: In a preregistered online experiment with a within-subjects design, I show that redistribution decisions by third parties are affected by loss aversion (therefore third-party loss aversion). Overall, spectators are twice as likely (i.e., 7 percentage points more likely) to choose a status quo over an alternative if the alternative results in a loss for one person, even if the alternative is favored by inequality aversion, maximin preferences and efficiency concerns. The effect is larger when the loss is higher compared to the gain and when the spectator's individual loss aversion is higher. The key contribution of the paper is disentangling third-party loss aversion from pure status quo preference, rank reversal aversion and other distributional preferences in multiple loss scenarios and linking it to individual loss aversion.

title: Tea Export Decline and Crime Activities in China
affiliations: Lingnan University, Nanjing University and Nanjing University - School of Business

detail.title: Tea Export Decline and Crime Activities in China
detail.abstract: Tea has been China’s major export product since the 17th century. This paper studies the effects of tea export decline on social instability in the late Qing Dynasty (1880−1894), with a focus on how a severe negative export shock turned clan-like quasi-blood mutual-aid organizations (i.e., Huidang) into criminal enterprises. The booming tea exports of British India and Ceylon in the 1880s caused a decline of China’s tea export to Britain, which serves as a natural experiment in our analysis. Using a panel data set of 266 prefectures in China, we find an interesting phenomenon: the tea export decline did not induce a significant surge in general crimes, but a special type of organized crimes (i.e., Huidang crimes) rose. Compared to other areas, Huidang crimes increased nearly fivefold in tea-growing areas after the tea export decline. Our finding suggests that Huidang served as a buffer against the negative export shock, but they eventually turned to crimes when the shock was too severe. The loss of work opportunities was a crucial channel through which the negative shock on tea exports impedes social stability. Clan culture and state capacity are also important mechanisms for understanding the impacts.

title: Adding Decision Problem Makes Information More Valuable
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Adding Decision Problem Makes Information More Valuable
detail.abstract: We consider decision-making under incomplete information about an unknown state of nature. We show that a decision problem yields a higher value of information than another, uniformly across information structures, if and only if it is obtained by adding an independent, parallel decision problem.

title: Preference Aggregation under Social Pressure
affiliations: and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Preference Aggregation under Social Pressure
detail.abstract: This paper studies preference aggregation in sequential majority voting with two candidates. Voters have heterogeneous preferences, are uncertain about the distribution of preferences, and incur a social-pressure cost from voting for the losing candidate. We characterize all symmetric Markov equilibria exhibiting a two-stage structure: a learning stage followed by herding once either candidate’s lead reaches a threshold. We characterize the conditions for equilibria existence and show that stronger social pressure and greater distributional uncertainty hinder preference aggregation. We also identify a class of resistant equilibria, in which voters become more willing to act sincerely as their preferred candidate falls behind, until herding begins. Finally, we study welfare across voting positions. An influence–risk tradeoff implies that early voters bear more risk but exert greater influence, while later voters are more protected but less influential. Consequently, although stronger social pressure reduces welfare for all voters, it makes later voters relatively better off than early voters within an equilibrium. Moreover, improvement in preference aggregation is not Pareto improving across equilibria.

title: Advancing Visual Interfaces: The Science, Engineering, and Market Dynamics of Liquid Crystal Displays

detail.abstract: Liquid Crystal Display (LCD) technology has evolved from a scientific curiosity into one of the most ubiquitous platforms in modern electronics, fundamentally shaping how humans interact with information and media. Initially discovered in the late 19th century and developed into practical applications in the 1960s and 1970s, LCDs rely on the unique electro-optical properties of liquid crystals to modulate light, forming individual pixels that collectively create highresolution images. Over the decades, advances in panel technologies including passive and active-matrix grids, Twisted Nematic, In-Plane Switching, Vertical Alignment, and Advanced Fringe Field Switching have enhanced colour reproduction, viewing angles, and response rates, enabling a wide array of devices from smartphones to large-format televisions. Critical materials, such as specialty glass substrates and indium-tin-oxide electrodes, have played a pivotal role in ensuring display stability, performance, and scalability. The integration of high-efficiency backlighting, pixel control mechanisms, and energy optimization has positioned LCDs as both cost-effective and highperformance solutions compared to legacy CRT and emerging OLED technologies.

detail.title: Effects of Excavation Loading Conditions on Ground Deformation and Stress Evolution in Plane-Strain Tunnel Simulations
detail.abstract: The construction of tunnels in urban areas typically affects a large number of buildings and infrastructure. The interaction between ground deformations induced by tunnel excavation and buildings or buried infrastructure is highly complex, and often requires numerical modeling for damage assessment. Despite recent advances in three-dimensional tunnel modeling, two-dimensional (2D) plane-strain analysis remain widely used in practice, particularly for TBM tunneling, because they are substantially simpler, computationally faster, and provides satisfactory results when the plane-strain simplification approximates the problem geometry. This paper investigates and compares three common loading conditions for simulating tunnel excavation using 2D plane-strain analysis: (1) the stress relief method (SR), (2) applied displacements at the tunnel perimeter promoting tunnel convergence while maintaining the invert position (AD), and (3) hydrostatic pressure applied at the tunnel perimeter (HP). The first two, SR and AD, are the most common excavation loading conditions in 2D numerical modeling of tunnels, whereas HP is commonly adopted in centrifuge modeling of tunnels. Centrifuge modeling results presented by Farrell (2011), Marshall (2009), and Zhou (2015) were used as reference data. These experiments encompass cover-to-diameter ratios (C/D) of 1.33, 2.0, and 2.44, relative densities of sand of 50% and 90%, and tunnel diameters of 4.67 m, 7.2 m, and 6.1 m. The centrifuge tunnel modeling results, conducted with HP excavation loading conditions, were satisfactorily replicated by all three excavation loading conditions using the Hardening Soil Model and the soil properties reported in Celestino et al. (2025). It was observed that: (1) for small tunnel volume losses (≈ 1%), the three excavation loading conditions provide essentially the same results; (2) for larger tunnel volume losses (≈ 2 to 4%), HP loading induces larger deformations at the tunnel crown, more pronounced dilatancy above the tunnel, and a narrower subsidence trough than SR and AD; and (3) SR and AD produce practically identical ground deformations above the tunnel, rendering the two excavation loading conditions equivalent for ground displacement predictions in the scenarios explored in this study. Thus, SR loading is recommended because it does not require prescribing tunnel convergence as an input for modeling and results in a more realistic radial stress redistribution around the tunnel perimeter compared to AD loading.

detail.title: Toward a Digital Twin for Wheel Loaders: Diagonal Recurrent Neural Networks for Online Soil Parameter Estimation

keywords.keywords: Soil parameter estimationTerramechanicsDiagonal recurrent neural networkEarthmoving machinesDigital Twin

detail.abstract: Accurate soil parameter estimation can improve mobility, localization, and traversability pre-diction for earthmoving machines. However, most terramechanics studies have limited practical applicability because they rely on laboratory testbeds and ignore terrain variability. This paper presents two diagonal recurrent neural network estimators in a digital twin framework for a wheel loader, based on a reformulated terramechanics model for on-site applications. One estimator recovers shearing parameters and the other bearing parameters. The main novelty is a sinkage-driven update mechanism that identifies the parameters influenced by sinkage and emphasizes estimator outputs. Soil parameters are updated by minimizing errors between measured and reconstructed driving torque and vertical load. The method is evaluated in an AGX Dynamics/Unity3D environment serving as the physical replica of the digital twin. For regolith, consistent estimation is achieved across flat and sloped terrains, with MAPE ranging from 0.66% to 5.39% and promising results for other materials against literature baselines.

title: Governing the Just Energy Transition in Bulgaria: Stakeholder Perspectives, Institutional Barriers and Regional Implications

detail.title: Governing the Just Energy Transition in Bulgaria: Stakeholder Perspectives, Institutional Barriers and Regional Implications
detail.abstract: This article examines the governance of the just energy transition in Bulgaria through an in-depth qualitative analysis based on semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders from public authorities, business, academia and civil society. While the European Union has established an extensive policy framework to support a socially just transition, empirical evidence on how these frameworks are interpreted and governed at national and regional levels remains limited, particularly in coal-dependent and institutionally constrained member states.Drawing on original interview material, the article analyses stakeholder perceptions of policy coherence, institutional capacity and social risks associated with the transition. The findings reveal that persistent policy uncertainty, institutional fragmentation and weak coordination across governance levels constitute major barriers to a just transition in Bulgaria. Rather than financial compensation alone, stakeholders emphasise predictability, transparency and trust as core dimensions of justice. Labour-related challenges, including skills mismatches and risks of social exclusion in coal-dependent regions, further highlight the importance of anticipatory and integrated governance approaches.By situating the Bulgarian case within broader debates on just transition, energy governance and socio-technical change, the article contributes new empirical insights from an under-researched EU context. It demonstrates how governance capacity shapes transition outcomes and underscores the need for stronger alignment between EU-level ambition and national and regional implementation.

title: A 5Ps-Based Forecasting Approach to Support Cleaner and More Balanced Sustainable Development Using SDG Indicators

detail.title: A 5Ps-Based Forecasting Approach to Support Cleaner and More Balanced Sustainable Development Using SDG Indicators
detail.abstract: This study analyzes regional trends and future trajectories of sustainable development using the Five Pillars (5Ps) framework, including People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership. Five composite pillar indices are constructed from the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) using regional data from 2000 to 2024. Two time series forecasting models, ARIMAX and linear regression combined with Holt Winters smoothing are applied to capture temporal dynamics and generate forecast results to 2030. The results reveal persistent regional disparities. With OECD members leading most pillars and Sub Saharan Africa remaining at the lowest levels. Forecasts indicate continued improvement in social and economic dimensions, while environmental sustainability and institutional stability show slower and more uncertain progress. These findings highlight the need for stronger and more balanced policy efforts to support sustainable development across regions.

title: Who Wants to be Rented? Rental Work and Digital Labour in the Age of AI
affiliations: University of Kashmir

detail.title: Who Wants to be Rented? Rental Work and Digital Labour in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: This paper looks at the new ways that AI agents are embodying in the real world. Through the case study of a platform called RentAHuman, this paper discusses how embodiment is leading to the development of haptic connections between AI agents and the real world, and its consequences on labour markets and the society. This paper examines the case of RentAHuman.ai, a platform that allows AI agents to hire humans as bodies to perform real-world tasks that the AI agent itself cannot execute. The paper discusses this phenomenon with respect to labour practices. This paper also employees a capitalistic critique of this practice, and proposes that hiring of humans by AI agents amounts to a modern form of serfdom as virtual entities cross into the real world. This paper finally attempts at conceptualising new class of digital labour, brought about by the potential of platforms such as RAH.

title: The Impact of Climate and Geopolitical Risk Indices on Tail-Risk Forecasting
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Impact of Climate and Geopolitical Risk Indices on Tail-Risk Forecasting
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether climate and geopolitical risk indices can improve Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall forecasts for financial markets. In this direction, we extend the semi-parametric Realized ES-CAViaR framework by incorporating news-based measures of physical climate risk, transition climate risk and geopolitical risk as additional risk drivers. Using daily data for the S&P 500 index, we assess out-of-sample forecasting performance through a comprehensive set of backtesting procedures, strictly consistent loss functions and the Model Confidence Set methodology. The results show that including climate and geopolitical risk measures significantly improves tail-risk forecasts at the 1% and 2.5% levels relative to specifications based exclusively on realized volatility. In particular, models combining geopolitical risk, physical climate risk and realized volatility consistently outperform alternative specifications across risk levels and evaluation criteria, indicating that these factors capture complementary sources of tail-risk. Overall, the findings underscore the relevance of climate and geopolitical risks for financial tail-risk modeling, with important implications for risk management and regulatory capital assessment.

title: Understanding the spatial structure of productivity: a hierarchical approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, GSSI, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Sapienza University of Rome - Dipartimento Metodi e Modelli per l'Economia, il Territorio e la Finanza

detail.title: Understanding the spatial structure of productivity: a hierarchical approach
detail.abstract: Productivity is unevenly distributed across space, yet hierarchical approaches have rarely been used to study its spatial organization. This paper proposes a spatially explicit framework that applies the size–rank relationship to productivity and operationalises three complementary new indicators to answer: (i) whether the national productivity hierarchy is reproduced locally (vertical integration), (ii) how productivity is organized within local systems (core–periphery structure), and (iii) whether local dominance is associated with systematic productivity advantages. By applying this framework to the Italian Local Labour Systems the paper reveals meaningful heterogeneity in local hierarchies of productivity, supporting the relevance of the proposed methodological approach for research and place-based policy interventions.

detail.title: Cloud Cover retrieval from all-sky images based on Neural Networks
detail.abstract: In this work, a new framework based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to predict Cloud Cover (CC) from sky images captured by all-sky cameras during both daytime and nighttime is presented. A new benchmark dataset, named GOA-ALLSKY, is created, comprising 4,500 training images and 900 validation images from Valladolid (Spain) and 900 test images from Lindenberg (Germany). These images are manually classified into CC in oktas by trained researchers and split into training, validation, and test sets. First, nine well-known CNN models are trained and validated using images from Valladolid. The ConvNeXt v2 architecture emerged as the best-performing model, predicting CC values that exactly matched the reference values in 78.67  \% of the cases. The mean bias error (MBE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) of the differences between the predicted and reference values are calculated, resulting in 0.00 oktas and 0.46 oktas, respectively, which is within the inherent uncertainty of human observers of 1 okta. Subsequently, the model is evaluated on the test set from Lindenberg to assess its generalization capability. However, in this set, a performance drop, revealing a domain shift, is observed in the nighttime subset of test images (50.89 \% accuracy). An analysis of the latent space through dimensionality reduction techniques identifies moonless nighttime images as the main source of error. To address this, a refinement strategy using a limited set of moonless nighttime samples from Fuencaliente (La Palma, Spain) is applied (180 images). A retraining strategy has been employed, including these moonless images. The refined model significantly recovers performance in the target domain without compromising the source domain accuracy (77.11 \% accuracy and RMSE about 0.46 oktas). In the final evaluation on the test set, the model achieves an accuracy of 71.30 \%, with an increase in nighttime accuracy of +17.55 \% and an RMSE and an MBE of 0.69 oktas and 0.05 oktas, respectively. These results demonstrate the robustness of the proposed framework for continuous, day and night automated CC monitoring across different sites.

title: Are we reaching the poor? Evaluating the targeting of Austria’s minimum income schemes via small area estimation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna and Austrian Institute of Economic Research (WIFO)

detail.title: Are we reaching the poor? Evaluating the targeting of Austria’s minimum income schemes via small area estimation
detail.abstract: This paper examines the targeting performance of anti-poverty cash transfers in Austria based on minimum income schemes. Over the past two decades, the Austrian social assistance framework has become highly fragmented, shaped by substantial discretion among the nine federal states as well as recurring and debated reforms.  Thus, our aim is to identify misalignments between beneficiaries, poor and eligible populations across federal states, household types, and over time. To this end,  we estimate the coverage rate and decompose it into two components, eligibility and non-take-up, to capture both the adequacy of eligibility rules relative to household characteristics and the behavioural dynamics underlying benefit claiming. Due to small sample sizes at disaggregated levels, we propose a small area estimation framework that enhances Austrian SILC and HFCS survey data with additional data sources. Our results suggest pronounced heterogeneity in targeting performance across states and household types and widespread undercoverage of poor households. Moreover, benefit claiming behaviours are broadly homogeneous across states, but heterogeneous across households, with childless households being less likely to claim it. These findings highlight key policy implications for strengthening the targeting of the measure.

title: Positioning sense of place in shaping adaptive behaviour in a flood-prone area: a case study of Kampung Melayu, East Jakarta
affiliations: Universitas Indonesia, Universitas Indonesia, Universitas Indonesia and Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa

detail.title: Positioning sense of place in shaping adaptive behaviour in a flood-prone area: a case study of Kampung Melayu, East Jakarta
detail.abstract: Climate change exacerbates the frequency and severity of flooding in urban informal settlements. While protection motivation theory (PMT) is widely used to understand flood-adaptive behaviour, current literature frequently models floods as static, rapid-onset events with contradictory findings regarding the role of place attachment by neglecting its overall status within the “sense of place” framework. Addressing this gap, this study explores how residents experience slow-onset disaster risks by employing a qualitative case study of Kampung Melayu, a highly exposed riverside settlement in East Jakarta, Indonesia. Based on 24 in-depth interviews and field observations, the findings reveal that inhabitants of Kampung Melayu experience fluvial flooding in a dynamic, gradual process, with environmental cues continuously generated as floodwaters rise. Residents cognitively decode these cues through a vernacular Siaga (alert) system and locally embedded place meanings, which, together with place attachment, constitute a more complete sense of place. This continuous appraisal process culminates in an "evacuation threshold"—a recursive psychological breaking point where residents constantly weigh escalating hazard noxiousness against the socio-economic risks of formalised evacuation. Viewed through this lens, local forms of adaptation such as delaying evacuation, vertical refuge, window-to-window evacuation, and flushing out riverine mud (nungguin air) are revealed as highly rational, context-specific PMT calculations. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that a shared sense of place harmonises individual threat appraisals, scaling individual self-efficacy up to a robust "community-efficacy". Therefore, these findings emphasise that effective disaster risk reduction policies must align with vernacular spatial adaptations rather than imposing top-down interventions that ignore local spatial realities.

title: Is Bitcoin Digital Gold? A Decadal Econometric Analysis of Cointegration and Risk Dynamics among BTC, Gold, and Crude Oil (2016-2026)

detail.title: Is Bitcoin Digital Gold? A Decadal Econometric Analysis of Cointegration and Risk Dynamics among BTC, Gold, and Crude Oil (2016-2026)
detail.abstract: The emergence of Bitcoin as a trillion-dollar asset class has sparked intense debate regarding its fundamental economic identity. Often touted as "Digital Gold," its proponents argue it serves as a robust hedge against inflation and systemic risk. This study investigates the longterm structural relationships and short-term volatility dynamics between Bitcoin, Gold, and Crude Oil over a rigorous ten-year horizon (2016-2026). Utilizing an extensive econometric framework-including Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests for stationarity, Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for normality, and Johansen Cointegration analysis-we examine whether Bitcoin functions as a "store of value" similar to precious metals or as a speculative asset. Our empirical findings decisively fail to reject the null hypothesis of no cointegration, revealing that Bitcoin, Gold, and Crude Oil do not share a structural macroeconomic equilibrium. Furthermore, the analysis of empirical distributions highlights severe idiosyncratic tail-risk native to cryptocurrency markets. These results provide critical insights for institutional portfolio diversification, suggesting that Bitcoin operates as an entirely independent asset class rather than a highly beta-leveraged commodity proxy.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of online trading platforms has redefined the landscape of global financial markets, bridging the gap between traditional brokerage systems and the digital era of investing. By leveraging real-time market data, automated execution tools, and multi-asset access, these platforms empower both retail and institutional investors to execute trades efficiently, manage portfolios intelligently, and respond to market dynamics with unprecedented speed. This report examines the evolution, types, regulatory frameworks, and functional features of online trading platforms, highlighting their impact on market accessibility, transparency, and investor behaviour. In addition, it explores contemporary innovations such as algorithmic trading, social trading, and cryptocurrency integration, while evaluating future trends that may reshape digital finance. Through an in-depth analysis of technological, strategic, and regulatory dimensions, this study offers a comprehensive understanding of how online trading platforms are transforming financial markets, driving democratization, and enabling sophisticated trading strategies.

title: Aquaculture displacement, not pollution treatment, drives coastal nitrogen decline in a tourism-dominated tropical island: Evidence from Hainan Island, China

detail.title: Aquaculture displacement, not pollution treatment, drives coastal nitrogen decline in a tourism-dominated tropical island: Evidence from Hainan Island, China
detail.abstract: Identifying the dominant drivers of coastal dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) remains challenging in rapidly urbanizing tropical regions where aquaculture, tourism, and sewage treatment co-evolve. This study links in-situ DIN measurements from 186 marine monitoring stations to a 7-year municipal panel (2017–2023) of 12 coastal municipalities across Hainan Island, China. Panel fixed-effects regressions, a Bartik instrumental variable (IV) strategy, a Spatial Durbin Model (SDM), mediation analysis, and placebo validation are deployed. Three findings emerge. First, marine aquaculture output is the dominant predictor of DIN across all methods (OLS: β = +0.084; IV: β = +0.091; SDM: β = +0.085; all p < 0.001), while sewage treatment capacity shows no detectable effect (p = 0.888). Second, tourism's apparent DIN-reducing effect (OLS: β = -0.030, p = 0.006) disappears under IV estimation (β = -0.018, p = 0.222), revealing it as a statistical artifact of aquaculture displacement rather than pollution treatment. Mediation analysis confirms 30% of tourism's apparent effect operates through aquaculture exit. Third, placebo tests confirm nitrogen-specificity: aquaculture shows no effect on DIP (p = 0.560) or COD (p = 0.053). City-level decomposition reveals Sanya's 72% DIN decline is attributable to aquaculture reduction, while Ledong achieved 80% DIN decline with zero sewage investment—solely through aquaculture exit. These findings indicate that environmental investment in coastal tourism cities is mis-targeted: priority should shift from point-source sewage treatment to aquaculture-derived diffuse nitrogen management.

title: Second-Order Predefined-Time Neural Networks for Sparse Recovery
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Second-Order Predefined-Time Neural Networks for Sparse Recovery
detail.abstract: Sparse signal recovery from limited linear measurements is a fundamental problem in compressive sensing and related inverse problems. It remains challenging due to its combinatorial nature and the lack of algorithms with guaranteed or explicitly controllable convergence times. In order to deal with this issue, in this paper, we study the continuous time neural dynamic approaches for solving the l0-norm sparse recovery problem. First, by modifying the WBP function, we give a smoothing approximation of the l0-norm, and then develop a convex relaxation of the sparse optimization problem. Second, by introducing the sliding technique, we propose a second-order time-varying predefined-time neurodynamic approach. And then we give some theoretical analysis, such as model equivalence, solution existence and predefined-time convergence. Third, a discrete-time counterpart of the proposed neural network is further derived, which is shown to inherit the predefined-time convergence in the sense of discrete time. Moreover, we develop a delayed second-order neurodynamic system and investigate its asymptotic stability. Finally, numerical experiments on sparse recovery and feature selection demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

detail.abstract: India's rapid digital-financial transformation has expanded credit access, accelerated consumption, and deepened financial inclusion. Yet beneath macroeconomic indicators of growth lies a persistent experience of financial strain among urban middle-class households. This paper introduces the concept of Engineered Insecurity to describe the structural interaction between retail credit expansion, algorithmically mediated consumption architecture, and household financialization. Drawing upon macroeconomic data, retail credit trends, inflation indicators, and behavioral economic theory, the study argues that financial vulnerability is not merely a cyclical by-product of economic shocks but is institutionally mediated within digitally embedded market systems. When platform incentive structures optimize engagement and transaction frequency, and when credit is seamlessly integrated into consumption interfaces, leverage expansion may be behaviorally intensified even in the absence of macroeconomic crisis. The paper concludes by proposing an architecture-aware regulatory framework aimed at strengthening household financial resilience in India's evolving digital economy.

title: Disturbed Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Deakin University, Deakin University and Deakin University

detail.title: Disturbed Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is now one of the popular control methods used in the area of robotics, which extends to various robotic domains including applications with teleoperation. Considering such applications, it is inevitable that random communication delay exist in between agent-environment interactions. This delay inevitably causes latency in capturing observations and actions. Moreover, noise can occur through external disturbances in RL entities such as rewards which will result in perturbed values. Tackling complex environments in such a scenario can be challenging as the agent receives noisy measurements amid possible delays. We take measures to address this issue in delay-aware RL by proposing a novel reward correcting filter into the delay handling RL framework. The proposed algorithm will estimate the original reward using available perturbed reward values, smoothing out the noise values present in the reward, making an accurate reward estimate available to the agent. We theoretically prove how the proposed filter can estimate the reward with regards to the monotonicity and convergence of the delay-aware RL framework, which in turn will tackle complex environments like robotic tasks. The validation of the algorithm is carried out with experimentations using the DeepMind Control Suite, which highlighted significant performance by showcasing the new algorithm’s robustness with perturbed rewards under delay-aware RL frameworks.

title: Global Input Sourcing and the Role of Supplier Risk

detail.title: Global Input Sourcing and the Role of Supplier Risk
detail.abstract: Is supplier risk --and the incentives to mitigate it-- a quantitatively important determinant of input sourcing? I build a trade model featuring cross-country differences in cost and risk, and analyze optimal sourcing decisions. Supplier risk is modeled as stochastic input prices correlated across countries, which firms mitigate through multi-sourcing. It addresses the prevalence of homogeneous goods imported to U.S. from multiple countries with price variations despite similar quality. Calibrating the model to match U.S. import decisions suggests that: 1. U.S. firms are risk-averse; 2. estimated supplier shock covariances decline with distance, implying a trade-off between low-cost but poorly-diversified nearby sourcing versus costly but well-diversified remote sourcing. Risk diversification explains a third of the observed variation in U.S. import shares across countries for intermediate inputs. In a simulation of the 2018-2019 U.S. tariff increase on Chinese inputs, China's share of U.S. imports declines by 25% more than without the diversification motive.

title: Exporting and Productivity Dynamics in the Chinese Footwear Industry
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Exporting and Productivity Dynamics in the Chinese Footwear Industry
detail.abstract: Revenue-based productivity measures confound physical efficiency with output prices. To recover physical productivity, I embed a CES demand system with destination-specific elasticities into a production-function framework and apply it to Chinese footwear firms from 2000 to 2006. After purging the price component, ordinary exporters are more productive than non-exporters. By contrast, pure processing trade firms, which account for more than half of all exporters, are substantially less productive, a pattern obscured by revenue-based measures. While revenue productivity shows no significant response to tariff reductions, physical productivity reveals sizable within-firm gains from trade liberalization. These findings imply that revenue-based evaluations overstate the performance of processing exporters and understate the productivity gains from liberalization.

title: TimesL: A Generic Hierarchical Framework for Mitigating Spectral Bias and Gradient Starvation in Time Series Forecasting
